data.title: Marianka – Barania lúka (Bazgovič), a Bronze Age hillfort above a quarry
data.excerpt: On the hill of Bazgovič above Marianka, an oval rampart surviving in places to a height of 3 m encloses some 8 ha, entered in the south through a pincer-shaped gate. The people of the Velatice culture built it, and J. Paulík's excavation of 1986–1990 recovered loom weights, spindle whorls, a bronze spearhead and a rare iron knife; the blade of a short sword from the quarry below remains a puzzle.
data.metaTitle: Marianka – Barania lúka, a Velatice culture hillfort
data.metaDescription: An oval hillfort of the Velatice culture (8 ha) on Bazgovič hill above Marianka, with a rampart up to 3 m high and a pincer-shaped gate; excavated 1986–1990.

children.text: The hillfort at Marianka is situated on a hill called Bazgovič, at an elevation of 384.5 m above sea level, above the present-day quarry. The site extends over a relatively flat spur of the Hrabovina, and the name of the site is sometimes given as Barania lúka. A small part of the hillfort in its summit area was destroyed by the quarry mentioned above.

children.text: The rampart, oval in shape and surviving in places to a height of as much as 3 m, protected an enclosure with an area of approximately 8 ha and measuring approximately 320 × 220 metres. In some places the course of the ramparts is already indistinct on the ground. The best-preserved rampart is on the eastern side of the site; in the south it ends at the original entrance into the fortified enclosure, the former so-called pincer-shaped gate, with the ramparts on both sides turned fairly sharply inwards. A tourist path from Bratislava to Záhorská Bystrica runs along the western rampart, with a branch to the well-known pilgrimage site of Marianka. The front part of the body of the original rampart was formed by a front wall built of quarried stones. The builders rested the wall against an earthen rampart heaped up behind it. The stone and earthen parts were tied together with horizontally laid beams. Although no ditch was dug in front of the front wall at Marianka, the descending slope provided sufficient protection, which was certainly strengthened by a palisade on the crest of the rampart.

The timber-and-earth ramparts on the Barania lúka eminence came to an end by fire. Juraj Bartík states that the extent of the burnt patch and the sporadic finds from the interior of the enclosure do not rule out the conclusion that the ramparts were burnt down by the inhabitants themselves as they left, taking their property with them.
Whom did the hillfort serve, and when?

The archaeological excavation at the hillfort took place in 1986–1990. The isolated oldest finds – a stone axe and sherds of vessels – belong to the Eneolithic. Later, in the Late Bronze Age, the site was settled by the people of the Velatice culture, who at that time lived not only in the Záhorie region but also in southern Moravia and Lower Austria. In chronological terms this is roughly the first two centuries of the second millennium BC, but the latest dating fragments testify to the so-called transitional Velatice–Podolí horizon. According to them the defences came to an end only in the years 1000 to 900 BC.

Evidence of the craft production of the people of the Velatice culture within the hillfort is provided by finds of loom weights and spindle whorls, which are connected with textile production. The metal component of the finds was supplemented by a bronze spearhead and a fragment of a sickle handle. A rare iron knife from the turn of the Bronze and Iron Ages also comes from the hillfort. Since numerous fragments of Late Bronze Age pottery occurred in the body of the rampart, we assume that the ramparts were built only in the later phase of the existence of the settlement. Apart from that, numerous pottery fragments were found on the hillfort, mostly with pronounced secondary burning.

In an article by J. Bartík and R. Bača from 2015 on the bronze swords of the Záhorie region it is stated that in 2012 the blade of a short sword was found in the quarry below the hillfort. It lay, however, on the first terrace of the quarry, where there was also various waste and building rubble that someone had brought to the spot without permission. It was therefore a secondary find spot, and it was not possible to determine whether the object had fallen into the former extraction pit from the higher-lying parts of the hillfort undisturbed by the quarry, or whether it had been brought here with the waste. We therefore do not know the original location, but we assume that it comes from the immediate vicinity. The blade is 39.4 cm long and weighs 195 g. It consists of 61% copper and 38% arsenic, with iron, nickel and vanadium represented in trace amounts. On the basis of its shape and dimensions the object from Marianka recalls some of the long daggers or short swords occurring over a wide area of Central Europe. Its attribution to the short swords of the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age is regarded as the least problematic solution to its dating, but even this remains open to question, since it is not a typical representative of a sword of that period, either in shape or in composition. On the blade we find neither rivet holes nor any final working of the edge by hammering or grinding, so it is clear that this is not a functional product but an unfinished blank. Nor can the possibility be ruled out that it served as a symbolic object without practical function, like the votive swords of the Bronze Age in Crete. In any case, the dating of the hillfort to the period of the Velatice culture does not agree with the presumed dating of the sword to the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age, and the sword will therefore probably always remain something of a mystery.
